seen-1.text:
Begum Rokeya (1880-1932) was a famous writer and a social worker. She lived in undivided Bengal in the early 20th century. She believed that women should have the same rights and opportunities as men have in the society. So she fought for their cause throughout her life.
Begum Rokeya was born in a village called Pairabondh, Rangpur in 1880. Her father Jahiruddin Muhammad Abu Ali Haider Saber was an educated landlord. Rokeya was married to Syed Sakhawat Hussain in 1897. Her husband was the Deputy Magistrate of Bhagalpur, now a district in the Indian state of Bihar. He was very cooperative, and always encouraged Rokeya to go on with her activities.
Many upper-class Muslims of Bengal at that time learnt Arabic and Persian as a medium of education and communication. But Rokeya had great love for her mother tongue. She learnt Bangla and English from her eldest brother Ibrahim.

seen-2.text:
It is easy to understand now that the global warming and climate change are caused by humans on earth. If we make least use of energy, the earth will be least polluted. The golden rule is, ‘Avoid machines as much as possible’. If your family has a car, use it less and walk to the shops. Walking and running are much more fun than sitting in a car. You may use bicycles too. You can save energy by changing your lifestyle. For example, you can often avoid the air-conditioning in summer and use hand fans instead. You can also use solar energy. It is free and more environment friendly. You can use energy-saving bulbs in your room. If you make a garden, you can grow much of your own food. You can also save the environment by reducing, reusing and recycling the things you use. The most important idea is if you don't buy so many things in the first place, you don't need to reuse or recycle them.
You can also save energy by turning things off when you don’t use them. People often leave lights, heating, air-conditioning, computers, TVs and gas burners on when they do not use them. Thus, they waste a lot of energy. Turning them off saves money too!
So, you can tackle climate change and live comfortably. There is plenty you can do. If we all work sensibly, we can save our lovely planet.
seen-2.reference: English For Today, Class 7, revised 2026; Unit Nine, Lesson 3 A; printed p.105; PDF p.110; Drive 1L1W-XCn_grZior6yOaoSkJ9eWviNIYP7

textbook-poems.text:
Whose Child is This? — Anonymous
“Whose child is this?” I asked one day
Seeing a little one out at play.
“Mine”, said the parent with a tender smile.
“Mine to keep a little while
To bathe his hands and comb his hair,
To tell him what he is to wear,
To prepare him that he may always be good
And each day do the things he should.”
“Whose child is this?” I asked again,
As the door opened and someone came in
“Mine”, said the teacher with the same tender smile.
“Mine to keep just for a little while,
To teach him how to be gentle and kind,
To train and direct his dear little mind,
To help him live by every rule
And get the best he can from school.”
“Whose child is this?” I ask once more,
Just as the little one entered the door.
“Ours”, said the parent and the teacher as they smiled,
And each took the hand of the little child.
“Ours to love and train together
Ours this blessed task forever.”
textbook-poems.reference: English For Today, Class 7, revised 2026; Unit Four, Lesson 4 A; printed pp.34–35; PDF pp.39–40; Drive 1L1W-XCn_grZior6yOaoSkJ9eWviNIYP7

In this fictional account, the students of a village school started a small seed library in February 2026. Their science teacher, Ms Rina, helped them collect and label seeds. Each packet showed the plant’s name and the month when it should be sown. Students could borrow a packet if they promised to return some seeds after the harvest. In March, twenty families joined the project. The students kept records in a notebook and visited a nearby farmer to learn how to store seeds in dry containers. By July, the library had forty packets of vegetable seeds. The club did not sell the seeds. Its aim was to share useful knowledge and encourage families to grow some of their own food. The students planned to add flower seeds the following year.

tasks.instruction: Answer any five of the following eight questions from the supplied textbook poem extracts.

subitems.text: Who first answers the speaker’s question in "Whose Child is This?"?
subitems.answer: The parent first answers and calls the child mine.

subitems.text: Name two things the parent does for the child.
subitems.answer: The parent bathes the child’s hands and combs his hair. The parent also tells him what to wear and prepares him to behave well.

subitems.text: What qualities does the teacher help the child develop?
subitems.answer: The teacher teaches him to be gentle and kind and guides his mind.

subitems.text: Why does the teacher keep the child "just for a little while"?
subitems.answer: The teacher cares for and educates the child during the time he is at school, rather than claiming permanent possession of him.

subitems.text: How many times does the speaker ask whose child it is?
subitems.answer: The speaker asks the question three times.

subitems.text: What happens when the child enters in the last stanza?
subitems.answer: The parent and teacher answer ours, smile and each take one of the child’s hands.

subitems.text: What does the change from "Mine" to "Ours" suggest?
subitems.answer: It suggests that the parent and teacher share responsibility for loving, guiding and educating the child.

subitems.text: What is the central message of the poem?
subitems.answer: A child’s growth is a shared, caring task for parents and teachers, who should work together.

tasks.instruction:
Read the opening and complete the story The Missing Library Book in at least ten new sentences. Give a suitable title.
Rafi borrowed a book from the school library. On the day he had to return it, he could not find it anywhere...
tasks.answer:
The Missing Library Book
Rafi searched his bag twice. Then he looked under his bed. The book was not there. He felt afraid that the librarian would be angry. For a moment he thought of making an excuse. Instead, he went to the library and explained the problem honestly. The librarian asked him to remember where he had last read it. Rafi recalled taking it to a group study session. He called his friend Salma after school. She checked the table where they had worked and found the book beneath a newspaper. Rafi thanked her and returned it the next morning. He apologised for the delay. From then on, he kept borrowed books in a separate place. He learnt that telling the truth was the first step towards solving a mistake.

tasks.instruction: Write a paragraph on A School Garden in about 150 words.
tasks.answer: A School Garden makes a school more attractive and gives students a chance to learn outside the classroom. Our garden is a small area beside the library. It contains flowers, vegetables and a few young trees. Students work in groups under a teacher’s guidance. We prepare the soil, plant seeds and water the beds according to a simple timetable. Labels beside the plants show their names and help younger students recognise them. The science teacher sometimes uses the garden to explain how plants grow and why insects are important. We also learn patience because a seed does not become a healthy plant overnight. Tools are kept safely, and we do not handle sharp equipment without adult supervision. The garden teaches cooperation as well as care for living things. When flowers bloom, everyone feels pleased. I think every school should have a garden if suitable space and safe conditions are available.

tasks.instruction: Write a dialogue between two friends about the benefits of reading books.
tasks.answer:
Rafi: You visit the library every week. What do you enjoy about reading?
Salma: Books introduce me to people and places I have never seen.
Rafi: Does reading help with schoolwork too?
Salma: Yes. It improves my vocabulary and helps me understand how ideas are organised.
Rafi: I sometimes choose a book that is too difficult and stop reading it.
Salma: You could begin with a short book about something you enjoy. The librarian can suggest one.
Rafi: Should I look up every unfamiliar word?
Salma: Not necessarily. First try to understand it from the sentence. Note important words and check them later.
Rafi: I spend a lot of time on my phone. How can I make time for books?
Salma: Set aside fifteen minutes before bed and keep a book near you.
Rafi: That sounds manageable. May I come to the library with you tomorrow?
Salma: Of course. We can choose different books and discuss them after reading.
Rafi: Thank you. I will give it a try.
